info.name: Mangal Superfoods API — Settings
info.description:
Application-level settings API for the Mangal Superfoods backend — the endpoints added in the `Setting` feature, separate from the main `postman-collection.json`.

**Base URL:** `{{base_url}}` — defaults to `http://localhost:4000`. All routes are under `/api/settings`.

### What this covers

| Method | Path | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| GET | `/api/settings` | public tier — the storefront's page-load call |
| GET | `/api/settings/private` | private tier — the frontend's post-login call |
| PATCH | `/api/settings` | update several groups at once, atomically |
| PUT | `/api/settings/:key` | update a single group |

### Two tiers

Public groups: `STORE_IDENTITY`, `SUPPORT_CONTACT`, `SOCIAL_LINKS`, `BUSINESS_HOURS`, `COMMERCE_CONFIG`. Private groups: `NOTIFICATION_CONFIG`, `INTEGRATION_CONFIG`.

The tier is decided by which object in `src/lib/settingsDefaults.js` declares the key. `Setting.isPublic` in the database only mirrors it and is never read to decide what to serve, so the tier cannot be changed over HTTP or by editing the column.

### The cache flag

Reads are served from an in-memory config. Pass `?cache=false` (or `{"cache": false}` in a JSON body) to force a fresh read from Postgres and replace what is cached. The match is **exact** on `'false'` — `'true'`, `'0'`, a typo, a repeated param and an absent param all serve the cache, and none of them is a 400.

### Authentication

**None.** This repo has no session/token middleware, so every route here is unprotected — including the private tier and the writers. "Private" means "not served in the anonymous storefront payload", **not** "access-controlled". Don't store secrets in the `Setting` table; they belong in `.env`.

### Before you run

1. `npm run prisma:db:seed` — creates the 7 setting rows. (The API works with zero rows too: values fall back to the code defaults.)
2. Restart the dev server if you just ran a migration — `src/lib/prisma.js` memoizes the client on `global.prisma`, which survives `--watch` reloads, so an old process keeps a client generated before `model Setting` existed.

Run the folders in order: **Read** → **Cache Flag** → **Write** → **Validation & Guards**. The Write folder ends with a cleanup request that restores the seeded values.

**Docs:** `docs/API_REFERENCE.md` (Settings section), `docs/DATABASE_SCHEMA.md` (Setting model).

item.name: Read
item.description:
Both read endpoints serve the in-memory config unless the request carries the cache flag, and both respond with `Cache-Control: no-store` so the in-process config stays the only cache.

The tier a group belongs to is decided by which object in `src/lib/settingsDefaults.js` declares it — `Setting.isPublic` in the database only mirrors that and is never read to decide what to serve.

Fetch the private settings tier. The frontend calls this immediately after a successful login, with `?cache=false` so it gets the private groups **and** refreshes the server's config in one round trip; it then merges the response into the public config it already holds.

exec: pm.test('Body flag forced a database read', function () {

request.description:
The flag is also read from a JSON body, where boolean `false` is accepted alongside the string.

**Caveat:** the query string is the primary channel because `fetch(url, { method: 'GET', body })` throws in browsers and in Bun, and proxies are entitled to drop GET bodies. Postman and curl will send it, so this request works — but prefer `?cache=false` from application code.

item.name: Write
item.description:
`PATCH /api/settings` is the primary writer: an admin screen edits several groups in one Save, and doing that as N sequential `PUT`s would mean N round trips, N cache refreshes, and a half-applied state if the third one failed. All groups go in one `prisma.$transaction`, and the config is refreshed once afterwards.

`PUT /api/settings/:key` is the single-group convenience form over the same code path.

Both **deep-merge**: nested objects merge key by key, while arrays and scalars replace wholesale (an element-wise array merge would mean removing the 2nd of 3 holidays leaves the 3rd behind). Run **Restore Seeded Values** at the end to leave the database as you found it.

exec: pm.test('All three groups were written', function () {
pm.test('Deep merge kept the siblings it was not asked to change', function () {
// currency.symbol changed; code and locale must survive
// untouched fields in the same group survive
// untouched fields in a patched group survive
pm.test('Response echoes only the groups that were touched', function () {

request.description:
Update several groups at once — note the batch spans **both tiers** (`SUPPORT_CONTACT` is public, `NOTIFICATION_CONFIG` is private).

Each value is deep-merged into what is stored, so `{"currency": {"symbol": "Rs."}}` changes the symbol and leaves `code` and `locale` alone. The response echoes the **effective** (merged) value of each group it touched.

`isPublic` in the body is ignored: the tier comes from the code defaults, which is what makes it untamperable over HTTP.

pm.test('Cached config already reflects the PATCH', function () {

request.description:
A plain cached read straight after the PATCH. It already shows the new values because the write refreshed the store — no `?cache=false` required.

**Caveat:** the config is per-process. A write refreshes only the instance that served it; another instance behind a load balancer, or a row edited in Prisma Studio, would stay stale until someone passes the cache flag.

request.description:
Single-group form, identical merge and validation behaviour to `PATCH /api/settings`. Reads better from curl and suits a one-field admin toggle.

`{{setting_key}}` defaults to `COMMERCE_CONFIG`. A field sent as `null` falls back to the code default rather than storing null, which is what guarantees callers never receive a null effective value.

exec: pm.test('Everything the folder changed is back to its seeded value', function () {

request.description:
Puts every field this folder changed back to its seeded default, so the folder is re-runnable.

Note `prisma:db:seed` will **not** do this for you: the seed's upsert deliberately omits `value` in its `update` branch, precisely so re-seeding cannot revert a real store address or shipping threshold to a placeholder. To reset the rows wholesale instead: `DELETE FROM "Setting";` then `npm run prisma:db:seed`.

item.name: Validation & Guards
item.description: There is no validation library in this repo, so validation is hand-rolled: a plain-object check, a known-key check, and key sanitisation. These requests cover each rejection path plus the two guards that matter — the tier cannot be promoted over HTTP, and a `__proto__` payload cannot pollute the process.

exec: pm.test('Every offending key is named at once', function () {

request.description: Unknown groups are rejected, and **all** of them are listed in one response. Rejecting one key at a time would make a caller fix a batch by trial and error.

exec: pm.test('Rejected on the bad key', function () {

request.description:
A batch mixing one valid entry with one unknown key. Every entry is validated **before** anything is written, so the valid half is not applied either — a partial apply is worse than a clean rejection. The next request proves it.

Beyond validation, the writes themselves run in one `prisma.$transaction`, so a failure part-way through the database work also leaves nothing applied.

item.name: Attempt to Promote a Private Group → ignored

exec: pm.test('Status code is 200 — the write itself succeeds', function () {
pm.test('isPublic is not echoed as a settable field', function () {

request.description:
Sends `isPublic: true` for a **private** group. The write succeeds (the empty `value` changes nothing) but the flag is ignored: `isPublic` is always derived from which defaults object holds the key, never read from the request.

The database column is only a mirror for readability — the code decides the tier — so there is no way to promote a private group over HTTP, and even editing the column by hand in psql would not do it. The next request confirms.

item.name: Verify the Private Group Is Still Hidden

exec: pm.test('Private groups are still absent from the public payload', function () {

request.description: Read fresh from Postgres and confirm the promotion attempt did not put a private group into the public tier.

exec: pm.test('The legitimate field was saved', function () {
pm.test('No __proto__ key survived into the stored group', function () {
pm.test('Nothing was grafted onto Object.prototype', function () {

request.description:
`JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{...}}')` produces an *own, enumerable* `__proto__` key that `Object.keys()` returns, and `express.json()` does not strip it. Anything that then walks the object and assigns into `target[key]` writes straight into `Object.prototype` and pollutes every object in the process.

`sanitizeKeys` removes `__proto__`, `constructor` and `prototype` at every depth from both request bodies and database rows, so the key never reaches the merge and is never persisted. The legitimate `salesEmail` in the same payload is saved normally.

Run **Restore Seeded Values** in the Write folder afterwards to clear `salesEmail`.
